record.paper_title: The Interiors of Uranus and Neptune: Current Understanding and Open Questions
record.original_question: Are Uranus and Neptune actually volatile-rich or water-rich planets, or can their observed properties be explained by rock-dominated compositions, so that the traditional label ice giants gives a misleading picture of both their bulk composition and the physical state of deep-interior material?

evidence.quote: Key fundamental questions regarding Uranus and Neptune remain open, such as: Key questions regarding Uranus and Neptune include: +Are Uranus and Neptune volatile-rich?
However, we actually do not know if the compositions of Uranus and Neptune are dominated by these materials, and even Pluto seems to consist of more rock than ice.
It was also shown that the planetary interiors are not necessarily water-rich, and that the measured gravitational field can be reproduced also if the planets are assumed to be rock-dominated.
We therefore propose that naming Uranus and Neptune sub-giants or outer-giants instead of ice giants is more appropriate.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider Uranus and Neptune, modeled as self-gravitating fluid planets in hydrostatic equilibrium and rotating with their measured rotation rates. For each planet the following observational constraints are given: total mass M, mean radius R, rotation period, and the low-degree zonal gravitational harmonics (J_2 and J_4). Allowed interior models consist of layered mixtures of three components — (i) hydrogen–helium gas with a protosolar He/H ratio, (ii) "ices" (a mixture dominated by H2O, with some CH4 and NH3), and (iii) "rock" (a silicate/iron mixture) — each described by a physically admissible equation of state at the relevant pressures and temperatures, with composition profiles required to be consistent with hydrostatic and thermal equilibrium.

Define a planet to be "volatile-rich" (or "water-rich") if, in every interior model that simultaneously satisfies all the above observational constraints to within their measurement uncertainties, the global mass fraction of the ice component exceeds that of the rock component by a definite margin (say, at least a factor of 2).

Question: Determine whether Uranus and Neptune are volatile-rich in the above sense. Equivalently, decide whether the set of admissible interior models compatible with the measured M, R, rotation period, J_2 and J_4 (and any other accepted observational constraints, such as atmospheric helium abundance and moment-of-inertia bounds) is contained in the volatile-rich regime, or whether it also contains rock-dominated models in which the rock mass fraction exceeds the ice mass fraction. Conclude whether the conventional designation of these planets as "ice giants" is justified by the data.
artifact.status_search_result: The composition of Uranus and Neptune remains an open question in planetary science. Recent reviews and modeling studies (post-2020) emphasize that current gravity-field data admit a wide range of interior structures, including rock-dominated solutions, and that the "ice giant" label may be misleading. No consensus determination has been reached; resolving the degeneracy is widely cited as a motivation for proposed Uranus and Neptune missions.

status_evidence.claim: The bulk composition of Uranus and Neptune (volatile-rich vs. rock-dominated) is explicitly listed as an open question.

status_evidence.title: Uranus and Neptune missions: a study in advance of the next Planetary Science and Astrobiology Decadal Survey
status_evidence.snippet: Fundamental properties such as bulk composition and internal structure of the ice giants are poorly constrained, motivating dedicated missions.
status_evidence.claim: Independent reviews confirm the bulk composition of the ice giants is not currently determined.
